questions.prompt: What is a cold call actually for?

options.text: To explain how Momence works
To find out their full budget
To earn the next conversation
To show we beat their software

questions.source: Day 5, "What a cold call is actually for"

questions.prompt: Which three things earn you the fifteen minutes?

options.text: Price, timing and authority
Relevance, interest and curiosity
Rapport, urgency and proof
Features, reviews and pricing

questions.source: Day 5, "What a cold call is actually for"

questions.prompt: In the six moments of a call, what comes right after "create relevance"?

options.text: Discover
Connect value
Ask for the meeting
Earn attention

questions.source: Day 5, "The anatomy of a great cold call"

questions.prompt: Two minutes in, the owner asks how Momence handles payments. What's the best move?

options.text: Walk her through payments, memberships and marketing
Tell her that's a question for the AE and move on
Answer briefly, tie it to her, then work toward the meeting
Email her a full feature sheet while you're still talking

questions.reveal: Answering is fine. Answering everything is the AE's job. One relevant thing, then move toward the meeting.
questions.source: Day 5, "Connect the problem to value" and "Pitch in the conversation, not at them"

questions.prompt: The owner is driving. She says she can't talk but asks you to call Thursday at 3. How did the call go?

options.text: A failure, since no meeting was booked today
A real outcome: you left with a callback time
Fine, but you should have pitched while you had her
Wasted, since it never reached discovery

questions.reveal: Some calls end at stage two, and that's a real outcome. A meeting, a name or a callback time, never nothing. And a callback is far more likely to book than a cold dial.

questions.prompt: She's described a problem and is now asking how other studios handle it. Where are you, and what's next?

options.text: Past value, so ask for the meeting now
Still in discovery, so ask three more questions
Back at the open, so re-introduce yourself
In the pitch, so cover the rest of the platform

questions.source: Day 5, "The full call flow" and "When you've earned the ask"

questions.prompt: A teammate says: "My calls go great. I explain everything Momence does and they say it sounds cool." No meetings. Best coaching?

options.text: Explain it faster so there's time left to ask
Add pricing so they can decide while on the call
Send an email first so they know it before you call
Stop selling the product and start selling the meeting

questions.source: Day 5, "You're not selling Momence. You're selling the meeting."

questions.prompt: Which three things should be true in the first ten seconds?

options.text: Say your name, title and the price range
Smile, slow down and give the pitch
Sound human, be clear, earn attention
Build rapport, find pain, show proof

questions.prompt: The owner picks up sharply: "Yeah? Who is this?" Which opener fits?

options.text: Friendly: build rapport with small talk first
Permission-based: get to the point fast
Discovery: ask about the whole schedule first
Pitch: lead with the full platform right away

questions.prompt: The person who answers sounds relaxed and happy to chat. Which opener fits?

options.text: Friendly: match her energy, then get to why you called
Permission-based: skip the chat and ask for the meeting
Pitch: she's open, so cover the platform while you can
Discovery: run through every question you prepared

questions.prompt: What's a gatekeeper's job, as Day 5 puts it?

options.text: Booking software demos for the owner
Screening out obvious spam calls only
Deciding which software the studio buys
Keeping you away from the decision maker

questions.prompt: The front desk asks: "What's this regarding?" What's the best response?

options.text: Give the full pitch so they can pass it along
Say it's a personal call so they put you through
Answer briefly, then ask for the owner by name
Ask them about their pain points to warm them up

questions.prompt: The person asking "what's this regarding?" knows the class schedule and current software in detail. What does that tell you?

options.text: They're a gatekeeper testing how much you know
You may already be talking to the decision maker
They want you to send an email instead of calling
They're about to end the call, so pitch quickly

questions.reveal: Some decision makers pretend to be gatekeepers. How much they know, and how much they're willing to share, gives it away.

questions.prompt: Your note says: Pilates, 14 weekly classes, one location, on MindBody. Which line creates relevance?

options.text: We help a lot of Pilates studios fill classes. Is that on your mind?
Momence is an all-in-one platform for wellness businesses like you.
Are you the owner, and do you have five minutes to hear about us?
I see you're on MindBody. Have you ever thought about switching?

questions.prompt: According to Day 5, research only becomes valuable when it does what?

options.text: Gets written into the AE handoff note in full
Covers every page of the business's website
Confirms the owner's LinkedIn profile is current
Changes what you say in the first thirty seconds

questions.prompt: Which question is designed to get the prospect talking first?

options.text: What's frustrating about your software?
How much are you paying each month?
How's your experience been with your setup?
Who makes the buying decisions there?

questions.prompt: The prospect says: "Honestly, scheduling's fine. It's the late cancellations that hurt." What do you say next?

options.text: Great. And how many instructors do you have?
How often does that happen, and what do you do now?
Our scheduling tools would make that even easier.
Got it. Can we set up a demo Thursday at 10?

questions.reveal: That's the thread: not scheduling, late cancellations. The answer was the next question. Most reps go to their next planned question and throw it away.

questions.prompt: The owner says no-shows are killing them. What's the best way to connect value?

options.text: Name one thing: reminders that cut no-shows
Run through the platform so she sees all of it
Quote how much revenue studios recover with us
Explain why her current software causes no-shows

questions.source: Day 5, "Connect the problem to value"; Day 6, no numbers on value

questions.prompt: Which three things does Day 5 say our owners care about?

options.text: Lower price, shorter contracts, faster setup
Better branding, a client app, more integrations
More reviews, more referrals, more awards
Fewer headaches, better retention, more revenue

questions.prompt: She told you what isn't working and asked how other studios handle it. What else do you need before you ask for the meeting?

options.text: Her agreement that Momence is better
A price she's comfortable paying
Nothing more. You've earned it, so ask
Answers to all your discovery questions

questions.reveal: The bar is low on purpose: something isn't working, she engaged, and there's one reason for a second conversation. She doesn't need to be sold or know the price.

questions.prompt: Which ask follows Day 5?

options.text: Would you maybe want to find some time to chat?
Let's set aside time Thursday at 10. Does that work?
How does your schedule look over the next while?
I'll send a link so you can pick any time you like.

questions.prompt: The owner says: "Sure, I'd be open to seeing it." What do you do?

options.text: Lock in a specific time right away
Share two more features so she's sure
Ask a few more discovery questions
Explain pricing so there are no surprises

questions.prompt: A good pitch on a cold call ends by doing what?

options.text: Listing the features that fit their business
Giving a price range for a studio their size
Pausing so they have time to think it over
Handing it back to them with a question

questions.source: Day 5, "Pitch in the conversation, not at them"

questions.prompt: What's the order of the Momence objection framework?

options.text: Disarm, Acknowledge, Ask, Add Value
Acknowledge, Add Value, Disarm, Ask
Acknowledge, Disarm, Add Value, Ask
Ask, Acknowledge, Add Value, Disarm

questions.prompt: Which of these is a brush-off rather than a real objection?

options.text: "It's too expensive for us."
"Just send me some info for now."
"Our last migration was a nightmare."
"We don't have the bandwidth to switch."

questions.prompt: The owner says: "Not a priority right now." What is that telling you?

options.text: You haven't earned attention yet, so earn it first
She has a real concern, so answer it with features
She means no, so log it as Dead and move on to the next
She wants a callback, so book one for three months out

questions.reveal: A brush-off tells you nothing about the offer, only that you haven't earned attention yet. An objection means answering the thing they raised. They're not the same move.

questions.prompt: What is the Disarm step for?

options.text: Proving their current software is the weaker one
Getting them to commit to a meeting on the spot
Finding out who really makes the buying decision
Lowering the guard they answered the phone with

questions.prompt: The prospect says: "We're happy with our current software." What's the best response?

options.text: Are you sure? A lot of studios find their software holds them back over time.
Okay, no worries at all. I'll send over an email with some info for you.
Glad it's working. I'm not here to uproot it. How much admin sits on top of it?
Most studios on that platform end up switching to us, so it's worth a look.

questions.reveal: Acknowledge, disarm, add value, ask, in about eight seconds. You're not trying to prove them wrong. You're reopening the conversation.
questions.source: Day 6, "How it sounds as one conversation" and "Redirect, don't debate"

questions.prompt: The owner says: "Bad timing. We're slammed this month." What's the best move?

options.text: No problem. I'll set you to Nurture and try again in a few months.
Totally fair. What's taking up your time the most this month?
I'll only take two minutes, I promise. Just hear me out on this.
That's exactly why you need Momence. Let me explain how it helps.

questions.prompt: You acknowledge, disarm and add value, then stop talking. What usually happens next?

options.text: They fill the silence with "just send me something"
They ask you to set up a meeting with the owner
They ask what Momence costs for a studio like theirs
They hand you over to someone who can decide

questions.source: Day 6, "Give the conversation somewhere to go"

questions.prompt: The owner says: "We tried switching last year and it fell apart," then keeps talking about what went wrong. Keep going or stop?

options.text: Stop: a failed switch means she'll never move
Stop: two objections means it's time to move on
Keep going, and push hard for the meeting now
Keep going: she gave a reason, not a refusal

questions.prompt: What are the two ways to add value in the framework?

options.text: Share a statistic, or tell a story about a similar studio
Offer a discount, or offer a free trial of the software
Ask a question about the value, or give the reason you called
Compare features, or compare the price against theirs

questions.source: Day 6, "Give them a reason to keep going"

questions.prompt: "Our software works just fine." Earlier in the call she mentioned she just hired a second instructor. What value do you add?

options.text: The admin that sits on top of her class scheduling
Managing more staff and more schedules as she grows
A quick rundown of everything the platform does
How much less she'd pay on Momence each month

questions.reveal: Acknowledge and disarm barely change from call to call. Value and the ask change completely, because that's where your pre-vetting and your listening show up.
questions.source: Day 6, "The framework holds. The words don't."

questions.prompt: What is parallel dialing for?

options.text: Cold, unworked leads only
Warm leads and callbacks
Hot leads who asked for a call
Any lead with a mobile number

questions.source: Day 7, "Let the reason pick the action"

questions.prompt: You're making plenty of dials but reaching very few people. What do you look at first?

options.text: Your opener and your first ten seconds
Your discovery questions and the thread
How you're asking for the meeting
Contact data, call timing and number type

questions.reveal: The number tells you where to look, never why. Before you add volume, check whether you're reaching the right people, with good data, at the right times.

questions.prompt: You connect often, but most people hang up within seconds. Where do you look?

options.text: Your contact data and calling times
Your discovery and objection handling
Your opener and your first ten seconds
Your daily dial volume and list size

questions.prompt: You have plenty of conversations, but few become meetings. What do you review?

options.text: Contact data, call timing and number type
Relevance, discovery, objections and the ask
Your dial volume and how many lists you run
Which hours of the day you open Orum

questions.source: Day 7, "Diagnose the conversion point first" and "Adjust before you add"

questions.prompt: In the daily loop, what is Orum's job?

options.text: Executing the strategy you already chose
Choosing which leads you work each day
Building your segments from your Book
Writing your notes after every call

questions.source: Day 7, "Orum executes the strategy. It doesn't create it."

questions.prompt: A prospect asked you to call back this afternoon. How should that call go out?

options.text: Parallel dial it with your cold list
Add her to an email sequence instead
Wait and let her call you back first
Power dial it, since she's warm

questions.source: Day 7, "Let the reason pick the action"
